name: Alitretinoin
lead: Alitretinoin (9-cis-retinoic acid) is a naturally occurring retinoid, a vitamin A derivative that activates both retinoic acid receptors and retinoid X receptors. It is a prescription medicine for visible skin disease: the oral capsules (Toctino) are used for severe chronic hand eczema that has not responded to potent topical corticosteroids, and the topical 0.1 percent gel (Panretin) is used on skin lesions of AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma.[1][2] It was developed by Ligand Pharmaceuticals.[1]

Its appearance relevance is clearing disease on the skin. In trials of severe chronic hand eczema, the treatment goal is clear or almost clear hands, with less redness, scaling, fissuring and thickened skin, and in Kaposi's sarcoma trials the endpoints were reduced size and redness of lesions.[2][4] It belongs to the same drug family as isotretinoin and tretinoin that people know from acne and skin-quality discussions, but it is used for different conditions, and it is not a cosmetic or acne product.[1]

Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication for oral use, and pregnancy prevention programmes apply where the capsules are approved. Common effects of the oral form are headache and raised blood lipids.[1][2]

Gel: US 1999, EMA 2000 for Kaposi's sarcoma; capsules: UK/EU 2008 for hand eczema[1]

paras: Alitretinoin is the 9-cis isomer of retinoic acid. Unlike all-trans retinoic acid (tretinoin), which acts mainly on retinoic acid receptors, alitretinoin binds all known retinoid receptor subtypes, three RAR and three RXR types.[2] RXRs were first identified as receptors that bind 9-cis retinoic acid, although whether it is truly an endogenous activator of them is still unclear; RXRs act as obligatory partners for several other nuclear receptors, which is why the compound has broad effects on gene transcription.[11] Wikipedia notes that it was once thought to be the natural ligand of RXRs, but later work did not detect its natural production in animal tissue.[1]
Alitretinoin can be made from all-trans retinoic acid by a palladium-catalysed reaction, and the two share overlapping pharmacology: it is partly isomerised to tretinoin in the body.[1]

Chronic hand eczema. The oral capsule was authorised in the UK and several EU states in 2008 for severe chronic hand eczema in adults that is unresponsive to potent topical corticosteroids; the UK granted prescribing on 8 September 2008, and NICE guidance in 2009 limited use to severe cases that had not responded to potent topical steroids, oral immunosuppressants or phototherapy.[1][2] Severe chronic hand eczema is a long-lasting, fluctuating condition that affects the hands and wrists and substantially affects quality of life.[12] German guidelines on hand eczema address its place in treatment, and a review of pompholyx, a blistering form of hand and foot eczema, describes alitretinoin as the most extensively studied systemic retinoid in hand dermatitis, with more limited experience in pompholyx itself.[3][13]

Kaposi's sarcoma. The topical 0.1 percent gel was approved in the US in 1999 for cutaneous lesions of AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma and by the EMA in 2000. It is not indicated when systemic therapy for Kaposi's sarcoma is required.[1] In two 12-week phase III trials, 35 and 37 percent of patients had complete or partial responses to the gel versus 18 and 7 percent with vehicle, according to a review.[14]
Other skin conditions. Alitretinoin has been tested in small studies in cutaneous lupus, mucosal lichen planus and hypertrophic lichen planus.[9][10][15]

Oral use commonly causes headache, raised triglycerides and cholesterol, and lowered HDL; common effects include dry skin, conjunctivitis, cracked lips, hair loss, anaemia and joint or muscle pain. Rare effects include benign intracranial hypertension and vasculitis, and tetracycline antibiotics combined with it can raise the risk of intracranial hypertension.[1] Mood effects, including depression and suicidal ideation, are listed on the label with unknown frequency.[1] Topical gel use commonly causes rash (reported in 77 percent of users), pain and itching at the site.[1]

Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication and nursing mothers should not use it; systemic use is to be avoided in women of childbearing potential who are not following pregnancy prevention.[1][2] The oral form is also contraindicated in liver insufficiency, severe kidney disease, uncontrolled raised blood lipids and hypervitaminosis A, and the capsules contain soya oil and sorbitol.[1] A clinical trial examined how alitretinoin affects the pharmacokinetics of an oral contraceptive.[16]

Alitretinoin modulates gene transcription via RAR and RXR, influencing cell proliferation and differentiation. In hand eczema it is described as reducing cytokine expression in keratinocytes and inhibiting dendritic cell maturation, which lowers T-cell activation.[1] A laboratory study reported that 9-cis retinoic acid modulates type I allergic immune responses.[17]

Oral absorption is variable and increases with food; it is highly protein-bound and metabolised in the liver by CYP3A4, with a half-life of roughly 2 to 10 hours, and is excreted mainly in urine and faeces.[1] Dermal application produces no significant systemic distribution.[1] A phase 1 trial registered the pharmacokinetics of oral alitretinoin in people with liver disease.[18]

Alitretinoin was once thought to be the natural ligand of retinoid X receptors, but later work did not detect its natural production in animal tissue.[1] Ligand Pharmaceuticals developed it, and a 2000 review described it as a retinoid receptor pan-agonist investigated in Kaposi's sarcoma.[1][14] The FDA approved the gel in 1999 and the EMA in 2000.[1] The oral capsule followed in 2008 for hand eczema, and the 2004 randomised trial of oral alitretinoin in 319 patients with refractory chronic hand dermatitis preceded its approval.[1][5]

The pivotal BACH trial was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in severe chronic hand eczema refractory to topical corticosteroids, testing 10 mg and 30 mg daily for up to 24 weeks.[4] Grokipedia reports that in this trial 47.7 percent of those taking 30 mg achieved clear or almost clear hands at 24 weeks versus 16.6 percent on placebo.[2] An earlier randomised placebo-controlled trial in 319 patients with refractory chronic hand dermatitis compared several doses with placebo, and a retreatment study examined patients with relapsed chronic hand eczema.[5][6]

Newer trials use alitretinoin as a comparator. DELTA FORCE, a 24-week, randomised, assessor-masked phase 3 trial at 102 centres, compared delgocitinib cream twice daily with oral alitretinoin once daily in adults with severe chronic hand eczema, with change in the Hand Eczema Severity Index at week 12 as primary endpoint; a 513-participant trial with a similar design is registered.[19][8] ALPHA, a randomised trial published in Health Technology Assessment in 2024, compared alitretinoin with phototherapy as first-line treatment.[20] A phase IIb study evaluated dupilumab in patients with an inadequate response to or intolerance of alitretinoin.[21]

A phase III vehicle-controlled study evaluated topical 0.1 percent gel in cutaneous AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma.[7] Registered trials include alitretinoin versus azathioprine in hand eczema, and small studies in cutaneous lupus and mucosal lichen planus.[9][10][22] A 2022 report described alitretinoin for hypertrophic lichen planus.[15]

card.summary: A prescription retinoid for severe chronic hand eczema (oral) and Kaposi's sarcoma lesions (gel), not a cosmetic.
card.note: Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication for oral use.

quick.overview:
Alitretinoin is a form of retinoic acid used as a prescription capsule for severe long-term hand eczema and as a gel for Kaposi's sarcoma skin lesions.

It treats skin disease; no source reviewed tested it for cosmetic purposes.
quick.mechanism: It activates both main families of retinoid receptors, changing gene activity that controls skin-cell growth and immune signalling.
quick.risks: Oral use can cause headache, raised blood lipids and dry skin and lips, and is contraindicated in pregnancy. The gel commonly causes local rash and pain.

chain: Oral alitretinoin capsule taken for severe chronic hand eczema
Retinoid receptor activation reduces keratinocyte cytokines and T-cell activation
Fewer inflamed, scaly, cracked patches on the hands
angle.text: For people whose hand eczema has resisted strong topical steroids, alitretinoin is a prescription option aimed at clearing the rash, scaling and fissures that mark the hands. Its payoff is skin appearance and comfort in a specific disease rather than general skin enhancement.
